tasks.instructions: Read the passage. Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D, for each question.

questions.prompt: Why did the town replace its streetlights?

options.label: A  Because residents complained about them
B  To reduce the cost of electricity
C  To reduce the number of road closures
D  Because the orange lamps were too bright

questions.prompt: What happened because residents complained?

options.label: A  The council removed the LED lamps
C  Shields were fitted and the lamps were dimmed at night
D  Workers replaced the lamps more often

questions.prompt: What does the sentence beginning “Although” show?

options.label: A  The changes cost some savings but reduced complaints
B  The changes increased the savings
C  The changes caused more complaints
D  The changes were made before the new lamps arrived

questions.prompt: Why do fewer roads have to be closed for repairs?

options.label: A  The lamps are dimmed after midnight
C  The council has fewer workers
D  The LED lamps last longer

questions.prompt: According to the council, what would have happened if the lamps had not been dimmed?

options.label: A  The savings would have been higher
B  More lamps would have broken
C  Complaints would have fallen faster
D  Roads would have been closed less often

questions.prompt: What does “As a result” introduce?

options.label: A  A contrast with the previous sentence
B  A consequence of the complaints
C  An example of the savings
D  A condition for the change

content.scope: Targeted IELTS preparation exercise; not a full paper.
content.mapping_scope: Task-specific reviewed focus with canonical English registry references. Not an IELTS/English equivalence or a pooled Academic Profile claim.
content.passage: Ten years ago, the town of Marlow Bridge replaced its old orange streetlights with white LED lamps. The main reason was cost: the new lamps use about half as much electricity. However, the change was not popular at first. Many residents said the white light was too harsh, and some complained that it kept them awake. As a result, the council fitted shields to lamps near bedroom windows and lowered their brightness after midnight. Although these changes reduced the savings slightly, complaints fell sharply. The council also found an unexpected benefit. Because the LED lamps last much longer, workers now replace them every twelve years instead of every four, so fewer roads have to be closed for repairs. If the lamps had not been dimmed, the council estimates that savings would have been ten per cent higher.
content.teacher_notes:
1 B — “The main reason was cost” (A is a later effect, not the reason).
2 C — “As a result, the council fitted shields … and lowered their brightness”.
3 A — concession: a small loss of savings, a large fall in complaints.
4 D — “Because the LED lamps last much longer … so fewer roads”.
5 A — third conditional: savings would have been ten per cent higher.
6 B — “As a result” follows the complaints.
Teach: underline each linking word and draw an arrow from cause to effect.
content.focus: Recognise logical relationships: cause, result, contrast, concession and condition signalled by linking words.

content.passage: Beekeepers in many countries have reported losing large numbers of honeybees each winter. Scientists have suggested several causes for this. One is a tiny parasite that attaches itself to bees and weakens them. Another is the loss of wild flowers, which means bees have fewer sources of food. Some farmers have responded by planting strips of flowers along the edges of their fields. These provide food from spring to autumn, and they also attract other insects that eat crop pests. A third cause may be the chemicals used to protect crops; although they are tested for safety, their combined effect on bees is less well understood. Researchers say that no single factor explains the losses. Instead, it is the combination that matters.

2 B — the parasite attaches itself.

content.passage: Many parents complain that their teenage children stay up late and are difficult to wake in the morning. It is easy to see this as laziness, but research suggests another explanation. During adolescence, the body releases the sleep hormone melatonin about two hours later than in childhood. In other words, teenagers are not choosing to feel awake at night; their bodies are. Some schools have moved the start of the school day from 7.30 to 8.30 a.m. In those schools, attendance improved and fewer students fell asleep in class. Of course, a later start creates problems for bus timetables and after-school sports. Even so, the evidence suggests that school times should take teenagers’ biology into account.
content.teacher_notes:
1 B — sets up the “laziness” view, then “but research suggests another explanation”.
2 A.
3 C — “In other words” restates.
4 D — evidence: attendance improved.
5 A — concession “Of course …”.
6 B — final sentence states the position.
Teach: purpose verbs — introduce, explain, illustrate, support, concede, conclude.
content.focus: Infer the writer's purpose: why a detail, example or sentence is included.

content.scope: Targeted IELTS preparation exercise; not a full paper.
content.mapping_scope: Task-specific reviewed focus with canonical English registry references. Not an IELTS/English equivalence or a pooled Academic Profile claim.
content.passage:
1. Trees make city streets cooler in summer. A single large tree can lower the temperature beneath it by several degrees, and shaded pavements stay cooler long after sunset.

2. Trees also improve people’s health. Patients in hospital rooms with a view of trees have been found to recover faster, and people living on tree-lined streets report less stress.

3. However, city trees are expensive to look after. Their roots can damage pipes and pavements, and dead branches must be removed before they fall.

4. Choosing the right species reduces these costs. Some trees have deep roots that stay away from pipes, and others drop few branches.

5. Many cities now ask residents to help. In some places, people can adopt a tree and water it during dry weeks.

6. Planting more trees will not solve every city problem, but their benefits are greater than their costs.
content.teacher_notes:
Main points are the first sentence of each paragraph here; the other options are supporting details (B, C in 1; A, C in 2 …) or come from other paragraphs.
6: A misreads “will not solve every city problem”.
Teach: ask “what does the rest of the paragraph prove?”
content.focus: Distinguish main and supporting ideas: tell the point of a paragraph from the examples and details that support it.

tasks.title: Working from home: main point or detail?
tasks.instructions: Read the passage. For each paragraph, choose the letter, A, B, C or D, that gives its MAIN point. The other options are details or ideas from elsewhere. Work on your own, without notes, a dictionary or help. Tell your teacher if anything interrupted you.
tasks.success_description: Find the sentence the rest of the paragraph explains or supports. Examples, numbers and reasons are usually supporting details.

questions.prompt: Paragraph 1

options.label: A  More than half of staff in some companies work at home two days a week
B  Staff work at home on Fridays
C  Working from home has become common

questions.prompt: Paragraph 2

options.label: A  Many employees feel more productive at home

questions.prompt: Paragraph 3

options.label: A  New employees rarely meet colleagues
B  Managers are concerned about teamwork
C  New staff learn from experienced colleagues

questions.prompt: Paragraph 4

options.label: A  Teams have meetings in the office
B  Training happens on office days
D  Agreed office days are a compromise

questions.prompt: Paragraph 5

options.label: C  Quiet areas are being added

questions.prompt: Paragraph 6

options.label: A  Experts know the long-term effects
B  Offices will return to the old pattern
C  The change is likely to last, although its effects are not yet known
D  Working from home is unpopular

content.scope: Targeted IELTS preparation exercise; not a full paper.
content.mapping_scope: Task-specific reviewed focus with canonical English registry references. Not an IELTS/English equivalence or a pooled Academic Profile claim.
content.passage:
1. In some companies, more than half of the staff now spend at least two days a week at home. Working from home has clearly become common in many offices.

2. Without a daily journey, employees start earlier, and they are interrupted less. Many say they are more productive at home.

3. Managers, however, worry about teamwork. New employees in particular may find it hard to learn from experienced colleagues they rarely meet.

4. Some firms have found a compromise. Teams agree on two “office days” each week when everyone comes in for meetings and training.

5. Offices themselves are changing as a result. Rows of desks are being replaced by meeting rooms and quiet areas.

6. It is too early to know the long-term effects, but few experts expect offices to return to the old pattern.
content.teacher_notes:
Note: in 1 and 2 the main point comes AFTER the supporting detail — students who always pick the first sentence will choose A in paragraph 1 and B in 2.
6: B reverses “few experts expect … return”.
Different text from R20; not a calibrated equivalent form.
content.focus: Distinguish main and supporting ideas: tell the point of a paragraph from the examples and details that support it.

tasks.title: Tourism in small towns: the writer’s views
tasks.instructions: Read the passage. Do the statements agree with the views of the writer? Choose YES if the statement agrees with the writer’s views, NO if it contradicts them, or NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks.
tasks.success_description: Look for the writer’s own opinion words (in my view, I believe, I am not convinced). Do not confuse the writer’s view with what “some argue”.

questions.prompt: Tourism is a simple way for small towns to become richer.
Visitors should be discouraged from coming to small towns.
Many tourism jobs are poorly paid.
Limiting the number of holiday rentals is an effective solution.
Holiday rentals should be taxed.
Tourists would be willing to pay higher prices.

content.scope: Targeted IELTS preparation exercise; not a full paper.
content.mapping_scope: Task-specific reviewed focus with canonical English registry references. Not an IELTS/English equivalence or a pooled Academic Profile claim.
content.passage: Tourism is often presented as an easy way for small towns to grow richer. In my view, this picture is too simple. It is true that visitors bring money to cafés and hotels, and I would not want to discourage them. But the jobs created are frequently seasonal and poorly paid, and house prices tend to rise as owners turn homes into holiday rentals. Some argue that local councils should simply limit the number of rentals. I am not convinced this works; in the towns I have studied, owners found ways around such rules. A better approach, I believe, is to tax holiday rentals and use the money to build homes for local workers. Whether tourists themselves would accept higher prices is a question I cannot answer.
content.teacher_notes:
1 NO — “this picture is too simple”.
2 NO — “I would not want to discourage them”.
3 YES — “frequently seasonal and poorly paid”.
4 NO — “I am not convinced this works” (the limit is what “some argue”).
5 YES — “A better approach, I believe, is to tax holiday rentals”.
6 NOT GIVEN — “a question I cannot answer”.
Teach: YES/NO is about the writer’s opinion, not facts in the world.
content.focus: Identify viewpoint and attitude: separate the writer’s opinion from other people’s views and from facts.

content.passage: Rental electric scooters have appeared in many cities, and opinions about them are divided. I think they are, on balance, a positive development. They allow people to make short journeys without a car, and they are cheaper than taxis. Critics say that scooters left on pavements are dangerous for pedestrians, and I agree that this is a real problem. However, banning scooters, as some cities have done, seems to me an overreaction. Requiring riders to leave scooters in marked parking areas would solve most of the difficulty. Some people also claim that scooters reduce air pollution, but I have seen no convincing evidence of this, since many riders would otherwise have walked.
content.teacher_notes:
1 YES — “on balance, a positive development”.
2 NO — “cheaper than taxis”.
3 YES — “I agree that this is a real problem”.
4 NO — “an overreaction”.
5 NO — “I have seen no convincing evidence”.
6 NOT GIVEN — who pays is not discussed.

tasks.instructions: Read the passage. Choose the meaning, A, B, C or D, of each word as it is used in the passage.

questions.prompt: “arid”
“laborious”

options.label: C  needing a lot of hard work

questions.prompt: “durable”
“sceptical”
“dispelled”

content.scope: Targeted IELTS preparation exercise; not a full paper.
content.mapping_scope: Task-specific reviewed focus with canonical English registry references. Not an IELTS/English equivalence or a pooled Academic Profile claim.
content.passage: In parts of North Africa, farmers have revived an ancient method of growing vegetables in arid land, where rain may fall only a few times a year. They dig deep pits and line them with stones, which stay cool and gather moisture from the night air. The technique is laborious: a single pit can take a family several days to build. Yet once completed, it is remarkably durable, lasting for decades with little repair. Agricultural experts were at first sceptical, doubting that such a simple system could feed many people. Their doubts were dispelled when harvests in a trial village tripled in five years.
content.teacher_notes:
1 A — “an ancient method” → brought back.
2 B — “rain may fall only a few times a year”.
3 C — explained after the colon: several days to build.
4 D — “lasting for decades with little repair”.
5 A — “doubting that …”.
6 B — doubts disappear when harvests triple.
Teach: underline the clue that proves each meaning.
content.focus: Infer word meaning from context: work out an unfamiliar word from the clues around it.

content.passage: For centuries, lighthouse keepers lived in isolated towers, often many kilometres from the nearest village. Their main task was to keep the lamp lit throughout the night, a duty they could never neglect, since a single dark hour might cause a shipwreck. Supplies arrived by boat, but in rough weather deliveries could be postponed for weeks. Keepers therefore stored enough food to be self-sufficient. Today, almost all lighthouses are automated, and the remaining towers are maintained by engineers who visit only occasionally. Some former keepers say they miss the solitude, although others admit that the life was monotonous.
content.teacher_notes:
1 C — “many kilometres from the nearest village”.
2 A — “a single dark hour might cause a shipwreck”.
3 D — “for weeks” in rough weather.
4 B — “therefore stored enough food”.
5 A — engineers only visit occasionally.
6 C — contrast with “miss the solitude”.
Different text from R24; not a calibrated equivalent form.
